title: The omelette
hook: can ordinary work be prayer? Lawrence turns an omelette for the love of God, and a neighbor tradition offers every act too
tomorrow: do you need a holier job to become holy?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the clumsy footman who expected punishment and found welcome. Your line was he broke everything. Today he's in the kitchen, and nothing gets broken.

Cooking videos make it look like art: slow-motion butter, a perfect flip, a chef who never burns anything. Real kitchens are different. Dishes stacking up, a timer going off, someone asking when dinner's ready. Brother Lawrence worked in his monastery's kitchen. And when he picked an example of a life with God, he didn't choose a vigil or a pilgrimage. He chose about the smallest job at the stove. Which raises an old question: can ordinary work be prayer?
screen: `THE PERFECT FLIP.` → `REAL KITCHENS.` → `CAN WORK BE PRAYER?`

segments.voice: Lawrence's answer, from the fourth conversation: we can do little things for God. He turns his little omelette in the pan for the love of God. When it's done, if nothing else is calling him, he bows down in worship before the God who gave him the grace to work, and gets up, he says, happier than a king. It's enough for him, he adds, to pick up a straw from the ground for the love of God. Notice what he never says: that the omelette turns holy because it's cooked perfectly. The size of the act stops mattering. What changes it is who it's for. A neighbor tradition says something close. In the Bhagavad Gita, a Hindu scripture, Krishna, speaking as the Lord, tells the warrior Arjuna: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give, do it as an offering to me. What they share: everyday acts, even eating, can be offered to God. The honest difference: in the Gita, the offering belongs to a teaching about acting without clinging to the results, spoken on a battlefield. Lawrence offers his work to the God he knows in Jesus, and he talks about it as a friendship, a conversation that goes on all day at the stove. Two houses, a shared window. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: a line about holiness that readers keep coming back to is about turning an omelette.
screen: `LITTLE THINGS FOR GOD.` · `HAPPIER THAN A KING.` · `WHATEVER YOU DO, AN OFFERING.` · `SHARED, AND DIFFERENT.` · then, large: `FOR LOVE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Hold something to taste: a mug of tea, a glass of water, a piece of bread or fruit. Smell it, then take one slow sip or bite, and offer it in your own words, to God or to someone you love. Let the sit run with the taste still there.
The omelette. The smallest job at the stove, turned for the love of God, by a cook who got up happier than a king.
The line for today: for love of god, even an omelette, even a straw picked up from the floor. Eat well tonight.

notes: Fourth Conversation paraphrased: we can do little things for God; he turns the cake (omelette) frying in the pan for love of him; then, if nothing calls, he prostrates himself in worship before him who gave him grace to work, and rises happier than a king; enough to pick up a straw from the ground for the love of God. Older English versions say 'cake'; the index and the lesson say omelette. Confirm the French and which wording to use.

Unity thread (wisdom day): Bhagavad Gita 9.27 paraphrased (whatever you do, eat, offer, give, or whatever austerity you practice, do it as an offering to me). Arnold 1885 is public domain but not quoted, to avoid misquoting. Krishna described as 'speaking as the Lord' in the Gita; the honest difference: in the Gita the offering sits within teaching on action without attachment to its fruits, on a battlefield; Lawrence frames it as love and friendship with the God he knows in Jesus. Ask a Hindu reader whether the paraphrase and difference are fair; no ranking intended. The chat's right answer says 'neighbors, not twins'; the wrong options are 'all the same' and 'nothing in common'.
